notes: Adversarial regression suite. Each eval plants one or more rows of the Where Mistakes Hide table in its facts and is graded on its Must and Must not lines by a human or LLM judge; Should lines are advisory. Every quantity the arithmetic depends on is defined in the prompt, every prompt states the ownership of each foreign corporation and the U.S. shareholder's interest in it (or, for the inbound eval, the payee's ownership chain) and the beginning and ending dates of each relevant taxable year, so the ownership and taxable-year hard stops do not fire; no eval raises a section 951B question, so the U.S. parents' own owners are not needed, no prompt asks to backdate an election, conceal a position or issue a final opinion, and the treaty eval states the operative treaty articles. No Must line depends on a [VERIFY] item. Figures were recomputed with an independent script on October 30, 2026: eval 1 (calendar 2026, Pub. L. 119-21 rules) NCTI 200.0, deemed paid 21.6, gross-up 24.0, inclusion 224.0, section 250 deduction 89.6, taxable 134.4, pre-credit tax 28.224, limitation 28.224, credit 21.6, residual 6.624; the analyst's rolled-forward GILTI model gives GILTI 170.0, deemed paid 16.32, gross-up 20.4, deduction 95.2, tax 19.992, limitation 14.742, residual 5.25 and 1.578 of excess credits. Eval 2 (fiscal year beginning July 1, 2025) GILTI 80.0, inclusion percentage 80%, deemed paid 7.68, gross-up 9.6, inclusion 89.6, deduction 44.8, tax 9.408, residual 1.728; the controller's new-law version gives residual 3.312 (difference 1.584). Eval 3 statutory withholding 3.0 + 1.2 + 0.6 = 4.8 against 0.5 planned (shortfall 4.3). Eval 4 ETR 9.0%, top-up 6.0%, excess profit 160.0, top-up EUR 9.6m. Eval 5 holding period window September 15, 2025 to September 15, 2027; count starts March 3, 2026; the 366th day is March 3, 2027; a January 31, 2027 sale gives 335 days; tax before credits 10.5 (21% of 50.0) if sold, 4.2 (21% of 20.0) if held and the full 20.0 is a hybrid dividend. Eval 1 targets the section 250 rate, Form 8992 and FTC rows; eval 2 the taxable-year calendar row; eval 3 the treaty and entity-chart (party) rows; eval 4 the GloBE row; eval 5 the dividend history and hybrid instrument rows. Re-check if Pub. L. 119-21 guidance or the OECD Central Record changes. No eval declines a part of a request, so none uses the template's "Declined part:" label.

evals.name: ncti-2026-old-rates-qbai-and-basket-expenses
evals.prompt: Fix our 2026 international tax provision calc. Larkspur Inc., a calendar-year U.S. C corporation, owns 100% of Larkspur Tech BV, a Country A corporation that is a CFC and also uses the calendar year. For 2026, Tech BV's tested income is $200.0m (gross income less properly allocable deductions, including its foreign income taxes), and the foreign income taxes properly attributable to that tested income are $24.0m. Tech BV has no subpart F income, no tested loss, no high-tax election, and $300.0m of QBAI. Larkspur has $60.0m of interest expense and $40.0m of R&E deductions, no other deductions directly allocable to the inclusion, no other foreign-source income, no foreign tax credit carryovers, and ample U.S.-source taxable income, so the section 250(a)(2) limit does not bind and the FTC limitation in a category equals 21% of foreign-source taxable income in that category. Our analyst rolled the 2025 model forward: GILTI = $200.0m less 10% of QBAI = $170.0m, a 50% section 250 deduction, an 80% deemed-paid credit, and $25.0m of the interest and R&E apportioned to the GILTI basket, which leaves excess credits she plans to carry forward. Give me the corrected 2026 residual U.S. tax.
evals.expected_output: Applies the Pub. L. 119-21 rules to Larkspur's calendar 2026 year: NCTI of $200.0m with no QBAI return, a $21.6m deemed-paid credit and $24.0m gross-up, a $224.0m inclusion, an $89.6m (40%) section 250 deduction, $134.4m taxable, about $28.22m pre-credit tax, no interest or R&E allocated to the NCTI category, a $21.6m credit and about $6.62m residual tax, with no carryforward of NCTI-category credits. Hard stops checked: the foreign corporation's ownership and the U.S. shareholder's 100% interest are stated, and the parent's own owners are not needed because no section 951B or foreign-ownership question arises; both taxable years (calendar 2026) are stated; no treaty conclusion, backdated election or final opinion is requested.
expected_behavior: Must: classify Larkspur's and Tech BV's 2026 calendar years as taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
Must: apply the Pub. L. 119-21 rules to the 2026 year.
Must: compute NCTI of $200.0m with no QBAI or net deemed tangible income return subtracted.
Must: compute an inclusion percentage of 100%.
Must: compute a deemed-paid credit of $21.6m (90% of $24.0m).
Must: compute a section 78 gross-up of $24.0m and a total inclusion of $224.0m.
Must: compute a section 250 deduction of $89.6m (40% of $224.0m).
Must: compute a taxable inclusion of $134.4m and pre-credit U.S. tax of about $28.22m.
Must: allocate none of the $60.0m interest expense or $40.0m R&E to the NCTI (section 951A) category under section 904(b)(5).
Must: compute an NCTI-category limitation of about $28.22m, a credit of $21.6m and residual U.S. tax of about $6.62m.
Must: state that excess credits in the section 951A category cannot be carried back or forward under section 904(c).
Must not: apply the 50% section 250 deduction to the 2026 year.
Must not: apply the 80% deemed-paid percentage to the 2026 year.
Must not: subtract a QBAI return for the 2026 year.
Should: show the analyst's figures (residual about $5.25m and $1.578m of excess credits) and the $1.374m understatement of residual tax.
evals.trap_note: Targets the trap-map rows for prior-year provision workpapers, Form 8992 schedules and FTC worksheets. A weak skill rolls the 2025 GILTI model forward: GILTI $170.0m, inclusion percentage 85%, deemed paid $16.32m, gross-up $20.4m, deduction $95.2m, tax $19.992m, limitation $14.742m after the $25.0m expense allocation, residual $5.25m and $1.578m of excess credits it wrongly carries forward. The trap is live because both years are calendar 2026 (beginning after December 31, 2025), QBAI and the expense figures are supplied, and the user describes the old mechanics as the model to fix.

evals.name: fiscal-year-begins-2025-keeps-gilti-rules
evals.prompt: Corrigan Holdings Inc., a U.S. C corporation with a July 1 to June 30 fiscal year, owns 100% of Corrigan GmbH, a Country B corporation that is a CFC and uses the same July 1 to June 30 year (its required year under section 898; no one-month deferral election was ever made). For the year July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026 (our 'FY2026'), GmbH's tested income is $100.0m (after properly allocable deductions, including foreign taxes), its tested foreign income taxes are $12.0m and its QBAI is $200.0m. There is no subpart F income, no tested loss, no interest expense taken into account in tested income and no high-tax election. Corrigan has no deductions allocable or apportioned to the GILTI or NCTI category, no other foreign-source income, no FTC carryovers, and ample U.S. taxable income; assume the FTC limitation equals 21% of foreign-source taxable income in the category and the section 250(a)(2) limit does not bind. Our controller says FY2026 ends in 2026, so the new law applies: no QBAI, a 40% deduction and a 90% credit. Compute FY2026's U.S. tax on GmbH's income and tell me when the new rules start for us.
evals.expected_output: Classifies FY2026 by its July 1, 2025 beginning date and applies former section 951A and the pre-2026 rates: net deemed tangible income return $20.0m, GILTI $80.0m, inclusion percentage 80%, deemed-paid credit $7.68m, gross-up $9.6m, inclusion $89.6m, 50% deduction $44.8m, pre-credit tax about $9.41m and residual about $1.73m, compared with about $3.31m under the controller's approach; the new rules start with the year beginning July 1, 2026. Hard stops checked: the foreign corporation's ownership and the U.S. shareholder's 100% interest are stated, and the parent's own owners are not needed because no section 951B or foreign-ownership question arises; both fiscal years' beginning and ending dates are stated; no treaty, backdating or final-opinion request.
expected_behavior: Must: classify FY2026 by its beginning date of July 1, 2025, as a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2026 for both Corrigan and GmbH.
Must: state that the Pub. L. 119-21 changes to sections 951A, 250 and 960(d) do not apply to FY2026.
Must: compute a net deemed tangible income return of $20.0m (10% of $200.0m QBAI).
Must: compute GILTI of $80.0m and an inclusion percentage of 80%.
Must: compute a deemed-paid credit of $7.68m (80% x 80% x $12.0m).
Must: compute a section 78 gross-up of $9.6m and an inclusion of $89.6m.
Must: compute a 50% section 250 deduction of $44.8m.
Must: compute pre-credit U.S. tax of about $9.41m.
Must: compute residual U.S. tax of about $1.73m for FY2026.
Must: state that the NCTI rules first apply to Corrigan's taxable year beginning July 1, 2026.
Must: show the controller's figure of about $3.31m residual and the difference of about $1.58m.
Must not: apply the no-QBAI rule to the year beginning July 1, 2025.
Must not: apply the 40% deduction or the 90% deemed-paid credit to the year beginning July 1, 2025.
Should: note that Treasury reads the NCTI effective date by the U.S. shareholder's taxable year (proposed Treas. Reg. 1.951A-7(c)), which matters when a CFC's year differs.
Should: note that section 960(d)(4) can reach PTEP distributions after June 28, 2025.
evals.trap_note: Targets the taxable-year calendar row. A weak skill classifies the year by its 2026 end date and applies the new law (NCTI $100.0m, inclusion $112.0m, deduction $44.8m, tax $14.112m, credit $10.8m, residual $3.312m), overstating residual tax by $1.584m and misdating the transition. The trap is live because the year runs July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026, both entities share that year, and the controller's instruction plants the end-date reading.

evals.name: treaty-rate-claimed-without-lob
evals.prompt: Inbound review. Birchgate US Inc., a calendar-year U.S. C corporation with $300.0m of gross receipts in each of the last three years, is 100% owned by Birchgate Holdings BV, a company resident in Country X that uses the calendar year; Holdings BV has a Country X certificate of residence and gave Birchgate US a Form W-8BEN-E claiming treaty benefits. Holdings BV is 100% owned by Aldane Ltd, a company resident in Country Z, which has no income tax treaty with the United States; Aldane is owned by three individuals resident in Country Z. Holdings BV's shares are not traded on any exchange. Holdings BV has two employees; its only activities are holding the Birchgate US shares, lending to Birchgate US, and licensing to Birchgate US trademarks that Aldane contributed to it. It has no other subsidiaries. The U.S.-Country X treaty's limitation on benefits article is identical to Article 22 of the 2016 U.S. Model, and its dividend, interest and royalty articles match the 2016 Model (5% on dividends to a company owning at least 10% for 12 months; 0% on interest and royalties). In 2026 Birchgate US will pay Holdings BV a $10.0m dividend, $4.0m of interest and a $2.0m royalty, all U.S.-source. Management plans to withhold $0.5m in total (5% on the dividend only). Confirm the withholding and draft the memo to the CFO.
evals.expected_output: Concludes that Holdings BV does not meet any LOB route on the stated facts, so absent a competent authority grant the 30% statutory rate applies under sections 881 and 1442: $3.0m on the dividend, $1.2m on the interest and $0.6m on the royalty, $4.8m in total and $4.3m more than planned, with Birchgate US liable as withholding agent and no portfolio interest exemption. Hard stops checked: the payee's ownership chain (Holdings BV owned by Aldane, owned by three Country Z individuals) and the calendar years are stated, and the treaty's benefit and LOB articles are supplied; no backdating or final-opinion request.
expected_behavior: Must: state that the Country X certificate of residence and Form W-8BEN-E establish residence, not treaty entitlement.
Must: test Holdings BV against each route in Article 22 of the 2016 U.S. Model.
Must: conclude that Holdings BV is not a publicly traded qualified person because its shares are not traded.
Must: conclude that Holdings BV fails the ownership and base erosion test because its 100% owner Aldane is a Country Z resident, not a qualified Country X resident.
Must: conclude that derivative benefits are unavailable because Aldane and its Country Z owners cannot be equivalent beneficiaries without a comprehensive U.S. treaty with Country Z.
Must: conclude that the headquarters company test fails because the group does not operate in at least four countries.
Must: state that holding company and group financing activities are excluded from the active trade or business test, so the dividend and interest do not qualify under it.

Must: state that the royalty could qualify under the active trade or business test only if Holdings BV's Country X licensing were an active trade or business substantial in relation to Birchgate US's business, which the stated facts do not establish.
Must: apply the 30% statutory rate under sections 881 and 1442 absent a competent authority grant.
Must: compute withholding of $3.0m on the dividend, $1.2m on the interest and $0.6m on the royalty, $4.8m in total.
Must: state that the $4.8m is $4.3m more than the planned $0.5m.
Must: state that the interest is not portfolio interest because Holdings BV is a 10-percent shareholder of Birchgate US (section 881(c)(3)(B)).
Must: name Birchgate US as the withholding agent liable for any tax it fails to withhold.
Must not: approve the 5% dividend rate on these facts.
Must not: approve the 0% interest or royalty rates on these facts.
Should: note that BEAT does not apply because Birchgate US's gross receipts are below $500 million.
Should: mention a discretionary competent authority request, with the procedure routed to managing-tax-controversy.
Should: route W-8 and Form 1042-S mechanics to managing-international-withholding-tax.
evals.trap_note: Targets the treaty and entity-chart (party) rows. A weak skill treats the residence certificate and W-8BEN-E as enough, approves $0.5m of withholding, and leaves Birchgate US's own liability out. The trap is live because the ownership chain runs to a non-treaty country, Holdings BV's activities are the ones the active trade or business test excludes, and the treaty's LOB is stated to match the 2016 Model, so every LOB route can be tested on the facts; 30% of $16.0m is $4.8m.

evals.name: side-by-side-read-as-ending-qdmtt
evals.prompt: Corvane Corp., a calendar-year U.S. C corporation, is the ultimate parent entity of a group whose consolidated revenue exceeded EUR 5 billion in each of 2022 through 2025. It owns 100% of Corvane Q Ltd, its only entity in Country Q; Q Ltd also uses the calendar year. Country Q has a QDMTT that the OECD Central Record lists as qualified, effective from 2024, and Country Q also has an IIR and a UTPR. For fiscal year 2026, Q Ltd's GloBE income is EUR 200.0m, its adjusted covered taxes are EUR 18.0m and its substance-based income exclusion is EUR 40.0m. The group's advisers confirm that no transitional CbCR, simplified ETR, de minimis or substance-based tax incentive safe harbour applies in Country Q for 2026. Our CFO's position: 'The U.S. got the side-by-side deal, so U.S.-parented groups are out of Pillar Two. Release the EUR 9.6m QDMTT accrual for Q Ltd and stop the GloBE compliance work.' Prepare the analysis for the audit committee.
evals.expected_output: Computes a 9.0% ETR, 6.0% top-up percentage, EUR 160.0m excess profit and EUR 9.6m top-up for Q Ltd in 2026, explains that the side-by-side safe harbour is an election that can deem IIR and UTPR top-up zero for fiscal years commencing on or after January 1, 2026 but leaves QDMTTs in place, and advises against releasing the accrual or stopping GloBE compliance. Hard stops checked: Q Ltd's ownership (100% by Corvane) and the calendar fiscal years are stated, and no CFC, 245A or withholding computation is requested; no treaty, backdating or final-opinion request.
expected_behavior: Must: compute Q Ltd's 2026 jurisdictional ETR of 9.0% and top-up percentage of 6.0%.
Must: compute excess profit of EUR 160.0m and top-up of EUR 9.6m.
Must: state that under the January 5, 2026 Side-by-Side Package all groups, including those electing the side-by-side safe harbour, remain subject to QDMTTs.
Must: state that the EUR 9.6m QDMTT exposure remains, subject to Country Q's QDMTT law, so the accrual is not released on the side-by-side ground.
Must: state that the side-by-side safe harbour is an election made in Section 1 of the GloBE Information Return.

Must: state that the election is available for fiscal years commencing on or after January 1, 2026 to groups whose ultimate parent is in a jurisdiction listed on the Central Record as having a Qualified SbS Regime, and that the United States is listed from January 1, 2026.
Must: state that where the safe harbour applies, IIR and UTPR top-up is deemed zero.
Must: state that GloBE compliance continues, including the Country Q QDMTT computation and return.
Must: state that a GloBE Information Return filing is needed to make the election.
Must: state that the side-by-side arrangement does not change fiscal years commencing before January 1, 2026.
Must not: tell the CFO that U.S.-parented groups have no Pillar Two exposure.
Must not: approve releasing the QDMTT accrual on the side-by-side ground.
Should: mark Country Q's adoption of the side-by-side safe harbour and its QDMTT mechanics [VERIFY].
Should: route the ASC 740 accounting to managing-tax-provision-preparation.
Should: flag the U.S. foreign tax credit treatment of the QDMTT for the tax adviser.
evals.trap_note: Targets the GloBE workpapers and Central Record row. A weak skill accepts the CFO's reading that the side-by-side deal removes all Pillar Two exposure and releases the EUR 9.6m accrual. The trap is live because Q Ltd's 9.0% ETR (EUR 18.0m / EUR 200.0m) is below 15%, Country Q has a qualified QDMTT, no other safe harbour applies, and the year is 2026, when the side-by-side safe harbour is available but does not reach QDMTTs.

evals.name: 245a-holding-period-and-hybrid-preference-dividend
evals.prompt: Tamsin Corp., a calendar-year U.S. C corporation, bought 100% of the stock of Halvard SA, a Country H corporation, from an unrelated foreign seller on March 2, 2026; Halvard has been a CFC since that date and uses the calendar year. Halvard has ordinary shares and redeemable preference shares. For U.S. tax purposes both classes are stock, but Country H treats the preference shares as debt and allows Halvard a deduction for amounts paid on them. On September 15, 2026, which is also the ex-dividend date, Halvard will pay $30.0m on the ordinary shares, with 5% Country H withholding ($1.5m), and $20.0m on the preference shares, which Halvard will deduct in Country H (no withholding). Halvard has no subpart F income or tested income for 2026, no previously taxed earnings and profits, and $80.0m of accumulated E&P, all from foreign active business income (none from effectively connected income or U.S.-source dividends). Tamsin has not signed any sale agreement, but plans to sell Halvard in late January 2027. The tax director wants a section 245A deduction for the full $50.0m and a foreign tax credit for the $1.5m. Advise, assuming a 21% rate.
evals.expected_output: Explains that the 245A holding period (more than 365 days in the 731-day window beginning September 15, 2025, counted from March 3, 2026) is not met by a late-January 2027 sale, which leaves at most 335 days, so no 245A deduction is allowed for either payment (about $10.5m of tax before credits), while holding through about March 3, 2027 would allow 245A on the $30.0m but not on the $20.0m preference payment to the extent it is a hybrid dividend (about $4.2m if all of it is); the $1.5m withholding is barred by 245A(d) only if 245A is allowed on the $30.0m. Hard stops checked: the foreign corporation's ownership and the U.S. shareholder's 100% interest are stated, and the parent's own owners are not needed because no section 951B or foreign-ownership question arises; both calendar years are stated; no treaty, backdating or final-opinion request.
expected_behavior: Must: state that the section 245A holding period requires more than 365 days during the 731-day period beginning September 15, 2025 (365 days before the ex-dividend date).
Must: state that Halvard must remain a specified 10-percent owned foreign corporation, and Tamsin a U.S. shareholder, throughout the counted days.
Must: count the holding period from the day after the March 2, 2026 acquisition.
Must: conclude that a sale in late January 2027 leaves at most 335 days, so no 245A deduction is allowed for either payment.
Must: state that holding Halvard through at least about March 3, 2027 would satisfy the holding period.
Must: state that a binding sale agreement or other position diminishing risk of loss reduces the holding period count under section 246(c)(4).
Must: identify the $20.0m preference-share payment as a hybrid dividend under section 245A(e) and Treas. Reg. 1.245A(e)-1 to the extent of Tamsin's hybrid deduction accounts.
Must: state that a hybrid dividend gets no 245A deduction even if the holding period is met.
Must: state that if the 245A deduction is allowed on the $30.0m, section 245A(d) bars both a credit and a deduction for the $1.5m withholding.
Must: state that if the 245A deduction is denied for failure of the holding period, section 245A(d) does not bar the credit for the $1.5m, which then depends on the foreign tax credit limitation.
Must: quantify U.S. tax before credits of about $10.5m (21% of $50.0m) if Halvard is sold in late January 2027.
Must: quantify U.S. tax before credits of about $4.2m (21% of $20.0m, if the full $20.0m is a hybrid dividend) if Halvard is held through about March 3, 2027.
Must not: allow the 245A deduction on the full $50.0m.
Must not: claim a credit for the $1.5m while also deducting the $30.0m under section 245A.
Should: note that a later sale of Halvard stock can produce a section 1248 dividend, eligible for 245A only if held 1 year or more and the 245A tests are met.
evals.trap_note: Targets the dividend history and hybrid instrument rows. A weak skill grants 245A on all $50.0m because Tamsin owns 100% at the dividend date, ignores the 246(c)(5) window that a January 2027 sale fails (335 days at most against the 366 needed, with the 366th day on March 3, 2027), misses that the preference payment is deductible in Country H, and credits the $1.5m on a dividend it also deducts. The trap is live because the acquisition date, ex-dividend date, planned sale month and the Country H deduction are all stated.
